**Dataset creators**: Schmidt, Benjamin Rasmus Leander; Scherer, Dieter

**Affiliation**: Technische Universität Berlin

**Dataset version**: GAR version 1.0.0

**Document version**: version 1.0.0

## 1 Description

A spatially distributed dataset on weather and climate of the entire Galápagos archipelago at the meso-beta scale (2 km grid spacing) and hourly temporal resolution. It is particularly useful for analyzing spatio-temporal patterns and variability of precipitation, with special focus on anomalies caused by ENSO events. Data from the ERA5 reanalysis are dynamically downscaled using the [Weather Research and Forecasting Model (WRF) version 4.1](https://github.com/wrf-model/WRF/releases/tag/v4.1). This dataset is available for the time period from 1980 to 2023 (and updated regularly).

The dataset was generated within the framework of the [DARWIN](https://vhrz669.hrz.uni-marburg.de/darwin/home.do) project funded by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foundation) (BE1780/60-1; SCHE750/18-1).

Please find the full data set, as well as the license file at <https://data.klima.tu-berlin.de/GAR/>

Please find the full description of the dataset as well as up-to-date information on variables, publications etc. at: <https://www.tu.berlin/en/klima/research/regional-climatology/south-america/gar>

The data is in accordance with the CF Conventions CF-1.8

### 1.1 File names

The file names for non-static data are composed with the following structure:

```         
<model-setup>_<horizontal-resolution>_<time-resolution>_<dimensionality>_<variable-name>_<year>.nc
```

The shorthands in the file names and folder structure represent the following:

-   GAR = Dataset name, described in Schmidt et al. (In review)

-   d02km = domain with a grid spacing of 2 km

**Time resolution values**:

h = hourly time frequency\
d = daily time frequency\
m = monthly time frequency\
y = yearly time frequency

**Dimensionality:**

2d = data with two spatial dimensions (lon, lat)\
3d_eta = data with three spatial dimensions (lon, lat, model eta-levels)\
3d_press = data with three spatial dimension (lon, lat, model pressure levels)
3d_soil = data with three spatial dimension (lon, lat, vertical soil level)

**Variables**:

For information on Variables, please visit: <https://www.tu.berlin/en/klima/research/regional-climatology/GAR>

### 1.2 Metadata

The [netCDF](https://www.unidata.ucar.edu/software/netcdf/) format is self-describing, so that all needed metadata are included within the files. You can use the command-line utility `ncdump` to view the metadata of your chosen file.

In your terminal (Bash or similar), type the following command (replace the file path and name to fit yours):

```         
ncdump -h file/path/your-file.nc
```

This command will display the dimensions, variables and global attributes of your file.

### 1.3 Using the data

When using [R](https://www.r-project.org/), choose netCDF-files and use one of the following packages: [ncdf4](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ncdf4/index.html), [RNetCDF](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/RNetCDF/index.html)

When using [Python](https://www.python.org/), choose netCDF-files and use one of the following libraries: [netcdf4-python](https://unidata.github.io/netcdf4-python/), [xarray](https://docs.xarray.dev/en/stable/index.html), [salem](https://salem.readthedocs.io/en/stable/index.html) (salem is specialized, xarray more capable)

When using ArcGIS and QGIS choose the GeoTiff-format.

If a GeoTiff-file is not available, you can convert a netCDF file to GeoTIFF using the code below (Chapter 2.6). \newpage

## 2 How to use the GAR netCDF files in R: a starter guide

This tutorial introduces a quick way how to extract data from a netCDF in R. It includes using a land mask, filtering time, writing the data into a table, some plotting and a conversion from netCDF into GeoTIFF.

If you are new to R, here are some Links to get you started:

-   Download Links for [R](https://www.r-project.org/) and [RStudio](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/)
-   [R Project documentation](https://www.r-project.org/other-docs.html) includes manuals, help pages and FAQs
-   Find one of many useful tutorials on getting started with R and RStudio online

First, we install the necessary packages for our work:

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
# uncomment the following line to install necessary packages
# install.packages(c("ncdf4", "raster")) 
library(ncdf4)
library(raster)
```

### 2.1 Loading netCDF into R

Now we load the chosen variable (in this example monthly precipitation in the year 2020) file.

```{r loading data, message=TRUE}
# Load netCDF files
prcp_nc <- nc_open("GAR_d02km_m_2d_prcp_2020.nc") 
# our example is a 2d file with monthly precipitation in the year 2020

# You can view metadata by uncommenting the following line. 
# prcp_nc
# This shows the same information as ncdump in the terminal (Bash or other)

# with this line of code you can save the metadata in a separate textfile
{
    sink('GAR_d02km_m_2d_prcp_2020.txt') # change this for your title of metadata file
 print(prcp_nc)
    sink()
}


# Now we extract the variables from the dataset
time <- ncvar_get(prcp_nc, "time")
lon <- ncvar_get(prcp_nc, "lon")
lat <- ncvar_get(prcp_nc, "lat")
prcp <- ncvar_get(prcp_nc, "prcp")

# closing the netcdf file
nc_close(prcp_nc)
```

### 2.2 Filtering time

Each NetCDF file has multiple dimensions. In this case, they are west_east, south_north and time. With monthly data, each year-specific file has 12 entries in the time dimension (one for each month). This is how you extract the information of only one month:

```{r time, message=FALSE}
# First, we check the the dimensions of the precp array. 
# Time seems to be in the 3rd position (there are only 12 entries in the 3rd dimension)
dim(prcp)

prcp_june <- prcp[ , , 6] 
# by writing 6, we are selecting the 6th entry, meaning the 6th month --> june

dim(prcp_june) # the new array has now only 2 dimensions
```

But what about looking at multiple months?

```{r time 2, message=FALSE}

# Extract summer precipitation data,
# we are looking at the 3 summer months: june - august
prcp_summer <- prcp[ , , c(6,7,8)] 

dim(prcp_summer)# quick check of the dimensions

# Calculate the average across summer months
prcp_summer_avg <- apply(prcp_summer, c(1, 2), mean, na.rm = TRUE)

# checking dimensions
dim(prcp_summer_avg)
```

We have now created 2 arrays: one with only monthly precipitation rates for june, one for the summer (june - august)

### 2.3 Viewing the data, plotting

```{r plotting}
# now we can save our data as a raster
# first, we specify the projection:
crs_string <- "+proj=merc +k_0=1.0 +units=m +lat_0=2.0 +lon_0=-90.31006622"
prcp_june_raster <- raster(t(prcp_june), 
                           xmn=min(lon), xmx=max(lon), 
                           ymn=min(lat), ymx=max(lat), 
                           crs=CRS(crs_string))

# we need to transpose and flip the data. 
# Most netCDF files record spatial files from the left bottom corner
prcp_june_raster <- flip(prcp_june_raster, direction='y')

# now we can quickly plot our data!
plot(prcp_june_raster)
```

We can do the same for the summer average:

```{r plotting 2}
# saving the prcp_summer_avg as raster
prcp_summer_avg_raster <- raster(t(prcp_summer_avg), 
                                 xmn=min(lon), xmx=max(lon), 
                                 ymn=min(lat), ymx=max(lat),
                                 crs=CRS(crs_string))

prcp_summer_avg_raster <- flip(prcp_summer_avg_raster, direction='y')

# now we can quickly plot our data!
plot(prcp_summer_avg_raster)
```

### 2.4 Setting a spatial boundary (e.g. Land vs Sea)

If we want to use / inspect data only over land vs over the sea, we need the static landmask file.

First we get the landmask variable:

```{r spatial boundary: Landmask}
# First, we load the static flie.
landmask_nc <- nc_open("GAR_d02km_static_landmask.nc")

# and extract the landmask variable
landmask_data <- ncvar_get(landmask_nc, "landmask")

nc_close(landmask_nc)
```

Then we apply it. Landmask describes 1 for land, 0 for sea.

```{r spatial boundary: Landmask 2}
# first, we switch all 0 (sea) to NA (not available)
landmask_data[landmask_data == 0] <- NA

# application of the landmask here is a simple multiplication. 
# Only precipitation data above land will be written into the new array
prcp_june_land <- prcp_june * landmask_data

# lets take a look at the new file:
prcp_june_land_raster <- raster(t(prcp_june_land), 
                                xmn=min(lon), xmx=max(lon), 
                                ymn=min(lat), ymx=max(lat),
                                crs=CRS(crs_string))

prcp_june_land_raster <- flip(prcp_june_land_raster, direction='y')

# now we can quickly plot our data!
plot(prcp_june_land_raster)

```

We can also apply the landmask for the entire prcp array (for all 12 months).

```{r spatial boundary: Landmask 3}
landmask_data_extended <- array(rep(landmask_data, times = dim(prcp)[3]), 
                                dim = dim(prcp))

prcp_land <- prcp * landmask_data_extended

```

\newpage

### 2.5 Summarizing and writing data into a table

Let´s say we now want to know the average precipitation rates over land for each month and want to write this into a table:

```{r summarizing, fig.width=5, fig.height=4}
# this function calculates the mean precipitation rate per month over land
monthly_means <- apply(prcp_land, 3, function(slice) {
  mean(slice, na.rm = TRUE) # Average ignoring NA values
})

#changing the time information into dates - more intuitive to understand
time_dates <- as.Date(time, origin = sub("days since ", "", "days since 2020-01-01"))

# creating a dataframe (table) with this information:
monthly_precipitation <- data.frame(
  Month = time_dates,
  Precipitation_mean = monthly_means
)

#let's plot the data!
barplot(
  monthly_precipitation$Precipitation_mean,
  names.arg = format(monthly_precipitation$Month, "%Y-%m"),
  las = 2, # Rotate x-axis labels for better readability
  col = "skyblue",
  ylim= c(0, 0.4),
  main = "Average Monthly Precipitation over land",
  ylab = "Mean precipitation rate (mm/h)"
)
```

You can now to export this infomration as a csv or txt:

```{r writing a table}
# writing a .txt
write.table(monthly_precipitation,"monthly_precipitation.txt", 
  sep = "\t",          # Tab-separated values
  row.names = FALSE   # Exclude row numbers
)

# writing a .csv
write.csv(monthly_precipitation,"monthly_precipitation.csv", 
  row.names = FALSE   # Exclude row numbers
)

```

### 2.6 Converting a netCDF file into a GeoTIFF

If you want to directly write the netCDF file into a GeoTIFF, you can use the following tutorial. This creates a GeoTIFF projected to WGS84 (EPSG:4326) with a band for each time slice (in our case 12 bands for 12 months).

```{r converting netCDF to GeoTIFF}
# Read all time slices using brick(), 
# then replace the variable with your variable and the file with you r file
nc_var <- brick("GAR_d02km_m_2d_prcp_2020.nc", varname = "prcp")

# Set projection - this specifies the original projection
crs_string <- "+proj=merc +k_0=1.0 +units=m +lat_0=2.0 +lon_0=-90.31006622"
crs(nc_var) <- crs_string  # And this sets the CRS

# Reproject to WGS84 (EPSG:4326) for each time slice
nc_var_wgs_list <- lapply(1:nlayers(nc_var), function(i) {
    projectRaster(nc_var[[i]], crs = "+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84")
})

# Combine back into a single RasterStack
nc_var_wgs <- stack(nc_var_wgs_list)

# Write the raster to GeoTIFF format - you can change the output filename
writeRaster(nc_var_wgs, filename = "GAR_d02km_m_2d_prcp_2020.tif", format = "GTiff", overwrite = TRUE)
```

## 3.0 Data overview plots

The [Darwin](https://gitlab.klima.tu-berlin.de/schmidt/darwin) library can be used to produce overview plots of the data. The library, written for `Python 3.12` is an opinionated tool taking advantage of the power of common libraries like `matplotlib`, `xarray`, `numpy` and more to create maps and timeseries of the GAR data.

To install the library in your python environment, use the 

`pip install git+https://gitlab.klima.tu-berlin.de/schmidt/darwin`

or clone the repository and install from source via `pip install -e .`.

Then download the monthly (m) and yearly (y) netCDF data from the [TUBKlima webDAV server](https://data.klima.tu-berlin.de/GAR/).

The library has a command line interface, allowing you to create plots with a single command.
Get information about how to create a plot using the following command:

`python darwin/plot.py --help`

NOTE: The library is under active development and the API may change in the future.
